\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle LMN\), so the corresponding sides are proportional.

\(\dfrac{AB}{LM} = \dfrac{BC}{MN} = \dfrac{CA}{NL} = \dfrac{5}{4}\)

\(\therefore LM = \dfrac{4}{5}\times 5.5 = 4.4\) cm, \(MN = \dfrac{4}{5}\times 6 = 4.8\) cm, \(NL = \dfrac{4}{5}\times 4.5 = 3.6\) cm.

No vertex is common to the two triangles, so this is the method of Ex. (1): all three sides of each triangle are now known, so each triangle is constructed on its own.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg BC = 6 cm.

(2) Taking B as centre and radius 5.5 cm draw an arc; taking C as centre and radius 4.5 cm draw another arc. Name their point of intersection A. Draw seg AB and seg AC. \(\triangle ABC\) is ready.

(3) Draw seg MN = 4.8 cm.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius 4.4 cm draw an arc; taking N as centre and radius 3.6 cm draw another arc. Name their point of intersection L. Draw seg LM and seg LN.

\(\triangle LMN\) is the required triangle similar to \(\triangle ABC\).

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The vertex R is common to \(\triangle PQR\) and \(\triangle LTR\), so this is the method of Ex. (2) and Ex. (3): the points R, Q, T are collinear and the points R, P, L are collinear.

\(\dfrac{PQ}{LT} = \dfrac{QR}{TR} = \dfrac{PR}{LR} = \dfrac{3}{4}\)

\(\therefore\) the sides of \(\triangle LTR\) are longer than the corresponding sides of \(\triangle PQR\), and \(\dfrac{RT}{RQ} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

\(\therefore\) if seg RQ is divided into 3 equal parts, RT will be 4 such parts.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg QR = 5.4 cm. Taking Q as centre and radius 4.2 cm, and taking R as centre and radius 4.8 cm, draw arcs cutting each other at P. Draw seg PQ and seg PR. \(\triangle PQR\) is ready.

(2) Divide seg RQ into 3 equal parts: draw a ray from R on the side of line RQ in which point P does not lie, take points \(T_1, T_2, T_3\) on it such that \(RT_1 = T_1T_2 = T_2T_3\), join \(T_3Q\) and draw lines parallel to \(T_3Q\) through \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).

(3) On ray RQ fix point T such that RT is four of those equal parts, i.e. \(RT = \dfrac{4}{3}\times 5.4 = 7.2\) cm.

(4) Through T draw a line parallel to seg QP. Name the point where it meets ray RP as L.

\(\triangle LTR\) is the required triangle. As a check on the drawing, LT = 5.6 cm, TR = 7.2 cm and LR = 6.4 cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

\(\triangle RST \sim \triangle XYZ\), so \(\dfrac{RS}{XY} = \dfrac{ST}{YZ} = \dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\angle XYZ = \angle RST = 40^\circ\).

\(\therefore XY = \dfrac{5}{3}\times 4.5 = 7.5\) cm and \(YZ = \dfrac{5}{3}\times 5.7 = 9.5\) cm.

No vertex is common to the two triangles, so each is constructed on its own, as in Ex. (1). Here the given measures of each triangle are two sides and the angle included between them, rather than three sides.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg ST = 5.7 cm.

(2) At S draw a ray making an angle of \(40^\circ\) with ray ST. On that ray fix point R such that SR = 4.5 cm. Draw seg RT. \(\triangle RST\) is ready.

(3) Draw seg YZ = 9.5 cm.

(4) At Y draw a ray making an angle of \(40^\circ\) with ray YZ. On that ray fix point X such that YX = 7.5 cm. Draw seg XZ.

\(\triangle XYZ\) is the required triangle similar to \(\triangle RST\).

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The vertex A is common to \(\triangle AMT\) and \(\triangle AHE\), so the points A, H, M are collinear and the points A, E, T are collinear.

\(\dfrac{AM}{AH} = \dfrac{MT}{HE} = \dfrac{AT}{AE} = \dfrac{7}{5}\)

\(\therefore\) the sides of \(\triangle AHE\) are shorter than the corresponding sides of \(\triangle AMT\), and

\(AH = \dfrac{5}{7}\times 6.3 = 4.5\) cm, \(AE = \dfrac{5}{7}\times 5.6 = 4.0\) cm, with \(\angle HAE = \angle MAT = 50^\circ\).

\(\triangle AMT\) has to be constructed first, because \(\triangle AHE\) is described only through it.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg AM = 6.3 cm. At A draw a ray making an angle of \(50^\circ\) with ray AM. On that ray fix point T such that AT = 5.6 cm. Draw seg MT. \(\triangle AMT\) is ready.

(2) Divide seg AM into 7 equal parts: draw a ray from A on the side of line AM in which point T does not lie, take 7 points on it at equal distances from each other, join the seventh of them to M and draw lines parallel to that segment through the other six.

(3) Name the end point of the fifth part of seg AM, counted from A, as H. \(\therefore AH = \dfrac{5}{7}\,AM = 4.5\) cm.

(4) Through H draw a line parallel to seg MT. Name the point where it meets seg AT as E.

\(\triangle AHE\) is the required triangle. Here both AH = 4.5 cm and AE = 4.0 cm turn out to be easily measurable lengths, so \(\triangle AHE\) can also be drawn directly from AH = 4.5 cm, \(\angle HAE = 50^\circ\) and AE = 4.0 cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a tangent to the circle, so the tangent at M is the perpendicular to radius PM at the point M. This is the worked construction '(i) Using the centre of the circle'.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre P and radius 3.2 cm. Take any point M on the circle.

(2) Draw ray PM.

(3) Draw line \(l\) perpendicular to ray PM through the point M.

Line \(l\) is the required tangent to the circle at point M.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The question does not name the centre, so let it be O. A line perpendicular to a radius at its outer end is a tangent, so the tangent at a point A of the circle is the perpendicular to radius OA at A. This is the worked construction '(i) Using the centre of the circle'.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 2.7 cm. Take any point A on the circle.

(2) Draw ray OA.

(3) Draw line \(l\) perpendicular to ray OA through the point A.

Line \(l\) is the required tangent to the circle at point A.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

Here the centre may not be used, so the tangent is drawn by the tangent- secant angle theorem, as in the worked construction '(ii) Without using the centre of the circle': if \(\angle CAB\) is an inscribed angle standing on chord CB, then the line CD drawn so that \(\angle BCD \cong \angle CAB\) is the tangent at C.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle of radius 3.6 cm. Take any point C on it. (The compass has to be opened to 3.6 cm to draw the circle, but the centre is not used anywhere in the construction that follows.)

(2) Draw chord CB and an inscribed \(\angle CAB\), where A is any other point on the circle.

(3) Taking A as centre and any convenient radius, draw an arc cutting the sides of \(\angle BAC\) in points M and N.

(4) Using the same radius and taking C as centre, draw an arc cutting the chord CB at point R.

(5) Taking the radius equal to d(MN) and R as centre, draw an arc cutting the arc drawn in step (4). Name their point of intersection D. Draw line CD.

Line CD is the required tangent, because seg MN and seg RD make \(\triangle MAN\) and \(\triangle RCD\) congruent by SSS test, so \(\angle BCD \cong \angle CAB\).

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The radius is 3.3 cm, so the diameter is \(2 \times 3.3 = 6.6\) cm — exactly the length of the chord asked for. \(\therefore\) the chord PQ is a diameter and the centre lies on it, i.e. the points P, O, Q are collinear.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.3 cm.

(2) Draw any line through O. Name the points where it cuts the circle as P and Q. Then PQ = 6.6 cm, so seg PQ is the required chord.

(3) Draw ray OP and draw a line through P perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at P.

(4) Draw ray OQ and draw a line through Q perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at Q.

Observation : the two tangents are parallel to each other.

Reason : the tangent at P is perpendicular to radius OP and the tangent at Q is perpendicular to radius OQ. Since O lies on seg PQ, ray OP and ray OQ lie along one and the same line PQ. Two different lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The radius is 3.4 cm, so the diameter is \(2 \times 3.4 = 6.8\) cm, while the chord MN is 5.7 cm. \(\therefore\) MN is not a diameter and it does not pass through the centre.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.4 cm.

(2) Take any point M on the circle. Taking M as centre and radius 5.7 cm, draw an arc cutting the circle at N. Draw chord MN.

(3) Draw ray OM and draw a line through M perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at M.

(4) Draw ray ON and draw a line through N perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at N.

Unlike the chord of the previous question, this chord is not a diameter, so ray OM and ray ON do not lie along one line. The two tangents are therefore not parallel — they meet each other at a point.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The radius is 3.4 cm and \(PQ = 5.5\) cm, and \(5.5 > 3.4\), so point Q lies in the exterior of the circle and two tangents can be drawn from it. This is the worked construction 'To construct tangents to a circle from a point outside the circle': a circle drawn with seg PQ as diameter cuts the given circle at the two points of contact, because an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre P and radius 3.4 cm.

(2) Take point Q such that PQ = 5.5 cm.

(3) Draw seg PQ. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg PQ to get its midpoint M.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius MP, draw a circle.

(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as A and B.

(6) Draw line QA and line QB.

Line QA and line QB are the required tangents. As a check on the drawing: the chapter's analysis notes that the triangle formed by the centre, the point of contact and the exterior point is right angled with the segment joining the centre to the exterior point as its hypotenuse, so \(QA = \sqrt{PQ^2 - PA^2} = \sqrt{5.5^2 - 3.4^2} = \sqrt{18.69} \approx 4.3\) cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The question does not name the centre, so let it be O, and let the given point be P, with OP = 7.3 cm. The radius is 4.1 cm and \(7.3 > 4.1\), so P lies in the exterior of the circle and two tangents can be drawn from it. This is the worked construction 'To construct tangents to a circle from a point outside the circle'.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 4.1 cm.

(2) Take point P such that OP = 7.3 cm.

(3) Draw seg OP. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg OP to get its midpoint M.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius MO, draw a circle.

(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as A and B.

(6) Draw line PA and line PB.

Line PA and line PB are the required tangents. As a check on the drawing: the triangle formed by O, A and P is right angled at A with seg OP as hypotenuse, so \(PA = \sqrt{OP^2 - OA^2} = \sqrt{7.3^2 - 4.1^2} = \sqrt{36.48} \approx 6.0\) cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The radius is 3.5 cm and OP = 5.7 cm, and \(5.7 > 3.5\), so point P lies in the exterior of the circle and two tangents can be drawn from it.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.5 cm.

(2) Take point P such that OP = 5.7 cm.

(3) Draw seg OP. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg OP to get its midpoint M.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius MO, draw a circle. It cuts the given circle in two points, because an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as A and B.

(6) Draw line PA and line PB.

Line PA and line PB are the required tangents. As a check on the drawing, \(PA = \sqrt{OP^2 - OA^2} = \sqrt{5.7^2 - 3.5^2} = \sqrt{20.24} \approx 4.5\) cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The centre may not be used, so the tangent is drawn by the tangent- secant angle theorem, as in the worked construction '(ii) Without using the centre of the circle'. Here the point of contact is A, so a chord AB and an inscribed angle standing on it are drawn, and that inscribed angle is then copied at A on the chord.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw any circle. Take any point A on it.

(2) Draw chord AB and an inscribed \(\angle ACB\), where C is any other point on the circle.

(3) Taking C as centre and any convenient radius, draw an arc cutting the sides of \(\angle ACB\) in points M and N.

(4) Using the same radius and taking A as centre, draw an arc cutting the chord AB at point R.

(5) Taking the radius equal to d(MN) and R as centre, draw an arc cutting the arc drawn in step (4). Name their point of intersection D. Draw line AD.

Line AD is the required tangent at A, because \(\triangle MCN\) and \(\triangle RAD\) are congruent by SSS test, so \(\angle BAD \cong \angle ACB\), which is the condition of the converse of the tangent- secant theorem.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The diameter is 6.4 cm, so the radius is \(\dfrac{6.4}{2} = 3.2\) cm, and R is at a distance equal to the diameter, i.e. \(OR = 6.4\) cm. Since \(6.4 > 3.2\), point R lies in the exterior of the circle and two tangents can be drawn from it.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.2 cm.

(2) Take point R such that OR = 6.4 cm.

(3) Draw seg OR. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg OR to get its midpoint M.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius MO, draw a circle.

(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as A and B.

(6) Draw line RA and line RB.

Line RA and line RB are the required tangents. As a check on the drawing, \(\triangle OAR\) is right angled at A with seg OR as hypotenuse, so \(AR = \sqrt{OR^2 - OA^2} = \sqrt{6.4^2 - 3.2^2} = \sqrt{30.72} \approx 5.5\) cm.

Here also \(OA = \dfrac{1}{2}\,OR\), so in the right angled \(\triangle OAR\) the side opposite \(\angle ARO\) is half the hypotenuse. That makes \(\angle ARO = 30^\circ\), and the angle between the two tangents \(60^\circ\). This last property is not stated anywhere in this chapter — it is the \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) result of the Pythagoras chapter — but it is a useful check on the finished drawing.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

An arc of measure \(100^\circ\) is an arc whose central angle is \(100^\circ\), so \(\angle APB = 100^\circ\). This chapter does not itself define the measure of an arc; that definition belongs to the chapter on the circle. The radius is not given, so any convenient radius may be taken.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre P and any convenient radius.

(2) Draw \(\angle APB = 100^\circ\) with its arms cutting the circle in points A and B. Then arc AB has measure \(100^\circ\).

(3) Draw ray PA and draw a line through A perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at A.

(4) Draw ray PB and draw a line through B perpendicular to it. This is the tangent at B.

The two tangents are the required lines. As a check on the drawing, they meet each other at a point, say X, and in the quadrilateral PAXB the angles at A and at B are each \(90^\circ\) while \(\angle APB = 100^\circ\), so \(\angle AXB = 360^\circ - 90^\circ - 90^\circ - 100^\circ = 80^\circ\).

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

E-F-A means that F lies between E and A. F is on the circle, so \(EF = 3.4\) cm and

\(EA = EF + FA = 3.4 + 4.1 = 7.5\) cm.

Since \(7.5 > 3.4\), point A lies in the exterior of the circle and two tangents can be drawn from it.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw a circle with centre E and radius 3.4 cm. Take any point F on the circle.

(2) Draw ray EF. On ray EF fix point A such that FA = 4.1 cm. Then EA = 7.5 cm.

(3) Draw seg EA. Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg EA to get its midpoint M.

(4) Taking M as centre and radius ME, draw a circle.

(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as P and Q.

(6) Draw line AP and line AQ.

Line AP and line AQ are the required tangents. As a check on the drawing, \(AP = \sqrt{EA^2 - EP^2} = \sqrt{7.5^2 - 3.4^2} = \sqrt{44.69} \approx 6.7\) cm.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

The vertex B is common to \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle LBN\), so the points B, A, L are collinear and the points B, C, N are collinear, and \(\angle LBN = \angle ABC = 40^\circ\).

\(\dfrac{AB}{LB} = \dfrac{BC}{BN} = \dfrac{AC}{LN} = \dfrac{4}{7}\)

\(\therefore\) the sides of \(\triangle LBN\) are longer than the corresponding sides of \(\triangle ABC\), and \(\dfrac{BN}{BC} = \dfrac{7}{4}\).

\(\therefore\) if seg BC is divided into 4 equal parts, BN will be 7 such parts, i.e. \(BN = \dfrac{7}{4}\times 4.8 = 8.4\) cm.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg BC = 4.8 cm. At B draw a ray making an angle of \(40^\circ\) with ray BC. On that ray fix point A such that BA = 5.1 cm. Draw seg AC. \(\triangle ABC\) is ready.

(2) Divide seg BC into 4 equal parts: draw a ray from B on the side of line BC in which point A does not lie, take 4 points on it at equal distances from each other, join the fourth of them to C and draw lines parallel to that segment through the other three.

(3) On ray BC fix point N such that BN is seven of those equal parts, i.e. BN = 8.4 cm.

(4) Through N draw a line parallel to seg CA. Name the point where it meets ray BA as L.

\(\triangle LBN\) is the required triangle. Note that \(LB = \dfrac{7}{4}\times 5.1 = 8.925\) cm, a length that cannot be set off accurately with a scale; the parallel line of step (4) produces it without its having to be measured at all. This is exactly the difficulty described in the chapter's 'For More Information' box.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.

\(\triangle XYZ \sim \triangle PYQ\), and the vertex Y is common, so X corresponds to P and Z corresponds to Q. \(\therefore\) the points Y, P, X are collinear and the points Y, Q, Z are collinear.

\(\dfrac{XY}{PY} = \dfrac{YZ}{YQ} = \dfrac{XZ}{PQ} = \dfrac{6}{5}\)

\(\therefore\) the sides of \(\triangle XYZ\) are longer than the corresponding sides of \(\triangle PYQ\), and \(YZ = \dfrac{6}{5}\times 7.2 = 8.64\) cm.

\(\therefore\) if seg YQ is divided into 5 equal parts, YZ will be 6 such parts.

Steps of construction :

(1) Draw seg YQ = 7.2 cm. Taking Y as centre and radius 6.3 cm, and taking Q as centre and radius 5.8 cm, draw arcs cutting each other at P. Draw seg YP and seg PQ. \(\triangle PYQ\) is ready.

(2) Divide seg YQ into 5 equal parts: draw a ray from Y on the side of line YQ in which point P does not lie, take 5 points on it at equal distances from each other, join the fifth of them to Q and draw lines parallel to that segment through the other four.

(3) On ray YQ fix point Z such that YZ is six of those equal parts, i.e. YZ = 8.64 cm.

(4) Through Z draw a line parallel to seg QP. Name the point where it meets ray YP as X.

\(\triangle XYZ\) is the required triangle. As a check, \(XY = \dfrac{6}{5}\times 6.3 = 7.56\) cm and \(XZ = \dfrac{6}{5}\times 5.8 = 6.96\) cm — neither of these is a length that can be set off directly with a scale, which is why the parallel line of step (4) is used instead of measuring them.

The construction itself is the answer; the book's answer section prints answers only for Problem set 4 Q.1.
